subject: templates to tame density code bloat?

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: templates to tame density code bloat?
parts:
Grab some coffee before reading this one.

I've been thinking a bit about what we can do
about the emerging problem Daniel's running into
adding the following to our densities:

1. error handling (default/user policy)
2. proportionality (no/[var/constant per arg])
3. truncation (lb/no, ub/no)

We know now how to use template metaprogramming to
reduce the choice of variable/constant per arg
for proportional calcs to a single function using
an is_var<T>::Yes templated class constant.

But now we have the same problem for the combo of
the other choices, especially the error policies,
which I suggested be factored into two forms, with
and without an error policy until all the compilers
catch up with template function defaults.

For instance, the road we're going down now has:

normal_log(y,mu,sigma);
normal_log(y,mu,sigma,error_policy);

normal_lb_log(y,mu,sigma,L);
normal_lb_log(",error_policy);

normal_ub_log(y,mu,sigma,U);
normal_ub_log(y,mu,sigma,U,error_policy);

normal_lub_log(y,mu,sigma,L,U);
normal_lub_log(y,mu,sigma,L,U,error_policy);

normal_propto_log(y,mu,sigma);
normal_propto_log(y,mu,sigma,error_policy);

normal_lb_propto_log(y,mu,sigma,L);
normal_lb_propto_log(",error_policy);

normal_ub_propto_log(y,mu,sigma,U);
normal_ub_propto_log(y,mu,sigma,U,error_policy);

normal_lub_propto_log(y,mu,sigma,L,U);
normal_lub_propto_log(y,mu,sigma,L,U,error_policy);

Given that we have around 20 densities, that's around
320 functions to write, document, and test. Gulp.

Maybe I've been reading too much Boost code and
too many template books, but how about a mega-template
solution. This is the kind of thing that general
policy types were meant to deal with.

We could have a single heavily templated function,
with a declaration like:

template <typename T_outcome,
typename T_loc,
typename T_scale,
typename T_lb,
typename T_ub,
bool Prop_to,
typename Policy>

inline calculated_return<T_outcome,T_loc,T_scale,T_lb,T_ub>::type

normal_log(T_outcome y,
T_loc mu,
T_scale sigma,

T_lb lb = stan::nil,
T_ub ub = stan::nil,

Policy p = default_policy<>::policy);

The same way we can use is_var<T_scale>::Yes to statically
compute if a variable is a parameter or a constant, we
can also define a templated class constant has_value<T_lb>::Yes
that will statically eval to true if T_lb has a value other
than a special dummy type stan::nil. We'd have to actually
complicate the calculated return a bit to coerce T_lb, but
that's doable:

calcuated_return<...,promotion_type<T_lb>::type,...>

which would evaluate to double if T_lb == nil.

I think we can drop the non-policy version, which would leave us
with a single function per density.

Now in the definition of normal_log(), we'll need some
heinous branching, which I wouldn't otherwise condone,
to wit:

normal_log(...) {
// error checking goes here; e.g., if sigma < 0,

calculated_result<...>::type lp(0);

if (!Prop_to)
lp += NEG_LOG_SQRT_TWO_PI;

if (!Prop_to || is_var<T_scale>::Yes)
lp -= log(sigma);

if (!Prop_to
|| is_var<T_out>::Yes
|| is_var<T_loc>::Yes
|| is_var<T_scale>::Yes)
lp -= 0.5 * square((y - mu)/sigma);

if ( (is_non_nil<T_lb>::Yes || is_non_nil<T_ub>::Yes)
&& (!Prop_to || is_var<T_lb>::Yes || is_var<T_ub>::Yes
|| is_var<T_loc>::Yes || is_var<T_scale>::Yes) {
if (is_non_nil<T_ub>::Yes && is_non_nil<T_lb>::Yes)
lp -= log(normal_cumulative(mu,sigma,ub,pol)
- normal_cumulative(mu,sigma,lb,pol));
else if (!is_non_nil<T_ub>::Yes && is_non_nil<T_lb>::Yes))
lp -= log(1.0 - normal_cumulative(mu,sigma,lb,pol));
else if (...)
lp -= ...;
else
lp -= ...;
}

return lp;
}


As before, all the conditionals will be defined statically.

The question is whether this is easier than writing 16 functions,
each of which looks like one path through this tangle of if-thens.

Also, having to set lp(0) is annoying, as it'll add another
auto-dif variable to the stack that's really useless.

We can combine the first two statements, to get

calculated_result<...>::type
lp(Prop_to : 0.0 : NEG_LOG_SQRT_TWO_PI);

but given that we're usually in the Prop_to case, this
isn't going to be much help in practice.

We could solve the problem with template expressions, but
I think that's going too far.

Another alternative would be to pass in an lp value to
increment. That works for our use case, at least, but it
adds a very complex calculated argument to the argument
list (I'd think it should go first), as in:

normal_log(calculated_result<...>::type lp,
T_outcome y,
T_loc mu,
T_scale sigma,

T_lb lb = stan::nil,
T_ub ub = stan::nil,

Policy p = default_policy<>::policy);

- Bob

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] templates to tame density code bloat?
parts:
Wow. Last night I was sort of thinking along the same lines then
thought the indirection might be too hard to follow for a new
programmer so gave up on thinking about it.

I am leaning towards making multiple functions. I think the API would
be cleaner if there was a single function per distribution, but I
think it may be hard to maintain if there is crazy branching within a
single large function. Although... perhaps we should consider having
the single entry point and having that dispatch to 16 different
functions? Especially if we can autogenerate the dispatching.

Hmm... for the time being, I'm going to continue to build out the
multitude of functions.


Daniel

parts:
After rereading the original email and Bob's comment on issue 14, I'm convinced we should template it out as suggested.

I'll finish out the Weibull distribution broken out so we can continue to build out more models, then I'll work on refactoring the distributions.

parts:
Back to the heavily templated function, we can't do that unless we
rely on C++0x. Should we go ahead and require it? I think last week,
we decided it caused too many problems in cross-compiler compilation.

I'm in favor of leaning on the new standard for the sake of not
maintaining double digit functions for each distribution.

Thoughts?

Daniel

>> >                    || is_var<T_loc>::Yes || is_var<T_scale>::Yes) {

parts:
Damn -- that's too bad.

We can use default arguments to functions, right?
I hope it's only a problem with pre C++11 compilers if
that default determines a template parameter. If
not, then I'm with you -- I'd rather not have to write
four base functions (+/- truncated above, +/- truncated below)
per density.

I'd rather not lean on compiler features that aren't
well supported yet. It'll do things like break
the interface from R in default installations and make
installing Stan a real pain.

So I think it'd be better to just have two functions:

foo_log(....) {
return foo(....,static_default_policy);
}

foo_log(...,policy) {
... real work here based on policy ...
}

That's what Boost does, so there's probably not a better
portable way to do it.

We could just implement the second and I could generate
code in Stan to include the default policies. But that
doesn't seem ideal if others might want to use our C++
API (which I don't think is out of the question given our
ability to do auto-dif).

My plate's pretty clear right now, so I can dive in and
help with these. Are you (Daniel) going to be around
tomorrow (Monday)? If so, I'd like to work on a single
class to get it in the right shape. After that, I think
the others should be pretty easy.

I'll try to read up a bit on Boost's metaprogramming as I'm
guessing they have all the stuff we'll need in place already.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] templates to tame density code bloat?
parts:
Default arguments to functions: no. Not without C++11 compilers. For example:

1) No default argument works:
template <typename Policy>
inline void
testFunction (const Policy& ) {
return;
}
...
testFunction (boost::math::policies::policy<>());

2) Default template argument works with C++11 compiler
template <typename Policy = boost::math::policies::policy<> >
inline void
testFunction (const Policy& ) {
return;
}
...
testFunction (boost::math::policies::policy<>() );
// DOES NOT WORK: testFunction ();

3) Default template argument and function argument works with C++11 compiler:
template <typename Policy = boost::math::policies::policy<> >
inline void
testFunction (const Policy& = Policy() ) {
return;
}
...
testFunction (); // THIS WORKS!
testFunction (boost::math::policies::policy<>() );

4) Does not work(even with C++11):
template <typename Policy >
inline void
testFunction (const Policy& = boost::math::policies::policy<>() ) {
return;
}
...
testFunction (); // Does not work.

I'll do some research to see if it's not well supported. We know that
it works with clang++ and g++ 4 in windows with an appropriate flag.
Wei had trouble with clang from Xcode 4, but maybe it was compiling
fine and it was a problem with the parser at that point?
